title: How Umami Works!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore umami, the fifth basic taste, starting with a banter about ketchup, tomatoes and mayonnaise. They cover Kikunae Ikeda's 1908 isolation of glutamate from kelp dashi, the later discovery of nucleotides (inosinate in bonito flakes, guanylate in shiitake), the basics of the gustatory system and how taste differs from flavor, the Western skepticism toward umami until the 1980s, and the evolutionary role of cooking and fermentation in umami intake. They also discuss MSG and the myth of "Chinese food syndrome," ways to add umami when cooking, and close with a listener mail from Meredith.

segments.title: Opening banter: ketchup, tomatoes and mayonnaise
segments.summary: The hosts joke around and discuss ketchup, the Vietnamese fish sauce origin of ketchup, mayonnaise, and eating raw tomatoes on burgers. They use this to lead into umami.

segments.title: Introducing umami and its history
segments.summary: Umami is introduced as the fifth taste, with the Japanese origin of the word meaning roughly delicious. The hosts describe it as a mild, musty flavor that enhances other tastes. They note Western scientists resisted it, and mention garum, the ancient Roman fish sauce.

segments.title: Ikeda's discovery of glutamate in dashi
segments.summary: Kikunae Ikeda, a chemist at the Imperial University of Tokyo, isolated the source of the taste from dashi. He found salts and then glutamate in kelp, and later a nucleic acid in bonito flakes. Akira Kuninaka later identified guanylate in shiitake mushrooms.

segments.title: Taste vs flavor and the gustatory system
segments.summary: The hosts explain how taste begins on the tongue with papillae and taste buds, which contain receptor cells. Receptors send electrical impulses to the nucleus of the solitary tract in the brain. Flavor adds smell, temperature, texture and memory to taste.

segments.title: Umami acceptance and receptors
segments.summary: Western skepticism delayed acceptance of umami until the 1980s, when an international symposium in Hawaii and studies identified specific G protein coupled receptors for umami. The hosts discuss how the receptors transduce chemicals into electrical signals and how umami compounds interact with sweet and salty tastes.

segments.title: Evolution of umami and cooking
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the evolutionary puzzle of umami. Receptors are ancient, but umami is mainly released by cooking or fermenting food, which breaks proteins into amino acids. They tie this to the role of fire and cooking in human brain development.

segments.title: MSG, health myths and cooking tips
segments.summary: The hosts discuss MSG's reputation, the claim of Chinese food syndrome, and evidence that MSG is not harmful. They mention hidden MSG ingredient labels, Umami Burger, and cooking tips such as roasting vegetables, caramelizing onions and adding parmesan rinds.

segments.title: Listener mail from Meredith
segments.summary: Meredith from Granite Falls, Minnesota writes about her hospital job scanning files and says the show keeps her company. The hosts respond and talk about making miso soup.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts mention the show's social media and website and sign off.
